claim: CR1 plays a key role in the control of complement activation and the immune clearance of C3b/C4b-coated immune complexes.
source: Complement Receptor One (CR1) plays a key role in the control of complement activation and the immune clearance of C3b/C4b-coated immune complexes (Krych-Goldberg and Atkinson, 2001).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Krych-Goldberg and Atkinson, 2001.

claim: CR1 is expressed on red blood cells, leucocytes and glomerular podocytes.
source: CR1 is expressed on a range of cells including red blood cells (RBCs), leucocytes and glomerular podocytes (Krych-Goldberg and Atkinson, 2001).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Krych-Goldberg and Atkinson, 2001.

claim: A number of CR1 polymorphisms have been described, including four molecular weight variants and variation in the number of CR1 molecules expressed on the surface of RBCs.
source: A number of CR1 polymorphisms have been described, including four molecular weight variants and variation in the number of CR1 molecules expressed on the surface of RBCs (reviewed by [Krych-Goldberg et al., 2002; Schmidt et al., 2015]).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to review articles by Krych-Goldberg et al., 2002 and Schmidt et al., 2015.

claim: Missense mutations of CR1 form the basis of the Knops blood group system of antigens.
source: Missense mutations of CR1 form the basis of the Knops blood group system of antigens, that includes the antithetical antigen pairs of Swain-Langley 1 and 2 (Sl1 and Sl2) and McCoy a and b (McCa and McCb) (Moulds, 2010).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Moulds, 2010.

claim: The non-synonymous SNPs A4828G (rs17047661) and A4795G (rs17047660) within exon 29 of the CR1 gene give rise to the Sl1/Sl2 and McCa/McCb alleles, encoding R1601G and K1590E, respectively.
source: The non-synonymous single nucleotide polymorphisms (SNPs) A4828G (rs17047661) and A4795G (rs17047660) within exon 29 of the CR1 gene give rise to the Sl1/Sl2 and McCa/McCb alleles, encoding R1601G and K1590E, respectively (Moulds et al., 2001) (Figure 1).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Moulds et al., 2001 and reference to Figure 1.

claim: The Sl2 and McCb alleles occur at high frequencies only in populations of African origin.
source: The Sl2 and McCb alleles occur at high frequencies only in populations of African origin (Figure 2) (Thathy et al., 2005; Zimmerman et al., 2003; Moulds et al., 2004; Noumsi et al., 2011; Fitness et al., 2004; Covas et al., 2007; Gandhi et al., 2009; Yoon et al., 2013; Hansson et al., 2013; Kariuki et al., 2013; Eid et al., 2010)
evidence: The claim is supported by multiple citations and reference to Figure 2 showing global allele frequencies.

claim: CR1 is a receptor for the invasion of RBCs by Plasmodium falciparum merozoites.
source: CR1 is a receptor for the invasion of RBCs by Plasmodium falciparum merozoites (Spadafora et al., 2010; Tham et al., 2010)
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Spadafora et al., 2010 and Tham et al., 2010.

claim: CR1 is a receptor for the formation of clusters of P. falciparum-infected RBCs and uninfected RBCs, known as rosettes.
source: CR1 is a receptor for the invasion of RBCs by Plasmodium falciparum merozoites (Spadafora et al., 2010; Tham et al., 2010) and for the formation of clusters of P. falciparum-infected RBCs (iRBCs) and uninfected RBCs, known as rosettes (Rowe et al., 1997).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Rowe et al., 1997.

claim: The rosetting phenotype is associated with severe malaria in sub-Saharan Africa.
source: The rosetting phenotype is associated with severe malaria in sub-Saharan Africa (Doumbo et al., 2009)
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Doumbo et al., 2009.

claim: Pathological effects of rosetting are likely due to the obstruction of microcirculatory blood flow.
source: The rosetting phenotype is associated with severe malaria in sub-Saharan Africa (Doumbo et al., 2009), with pathological effects likely due to the obstruction of microcirculatory blood flow (Kaul et al., 1991).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Kaul et al., 1991.

claim: RBCs from donors with the high-frequency African CR1 Knops mutations bind poorly to the parasite ligand P. falciparum erythrocyte membrane protein-1 (PfEMP1) that mediates rosetting by iRBCs.
source: RBCs from donors with the high-frequency African CR1 Knops mutations bind poorly to the parasite ligand P. falciparum erythrocyte membrane protein-1 (PfEMP1) that mediates rosetting by iRBCs, potentially protecting against severe malaria by reducing rosetting (Rowe et al., 1997).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Rowe et al., 1997.

claim: Some studies show an association between Sl and McC genotypes and severe malaria.
source: Nevertheless, epidemiological data supporting this possibility are contradictory, with some studies showing an association between Sl and McC genotypes and severe malaria (Thathy et al., 2005; Kariuki et al., 2013; Tettey et al., 2015)
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Thathy et al., 2005; Kariuki et al., 2013; Tettey et al., 2015.

claim: Some studies find no association between Sl and McC genotypes and severe malaria.
source: Nevertheless, epidemiological data supporting this possibility are contradictory, with some studies showing an association between Sl and McC genotypes and severe malaria (Thathy et al., 2005; Kariuki et al., 2013; Tettey et al., 2015) and others finding none (Zimmerman et al., 2003; Hansson et al., 2013; Jallow et al., 2009; Manjurano et al., 2012; Toure et al., 2012; Rockett et al., 2014).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Zimmerman et al., 2003; Hansson et al., 2013; Jallow et al., 2009; Manjurano et al., 2012; Toure et al., 2012; Rockett et al., 2014.

claim: Data were obtained from 5545 children enrolled in a case-control study of severe malaria.
source: Data were obtained from 5545 children enrolled in a case-control study of severe malaria (Figure 3).
evidence: The claim is supported by reference to Figure 3 showing the study enrollment.

claim: The Sl2 allele frequency in the Kenyan study population was 0.68.
source: The Sl2 and McCb allele frequencies (0.68 and 0.16 respectively) were comparable to other African populations (Figure 2).
evidence: The claim is directly stated in the text with a specific frequency value.

claim: The McCb allele frequency in the Kenyan study population was 0.16.
source: The Sl2 and McCb allele frequencies (0.68 and 0.16 respectively) were comparable to other African populations (Figure 2).
evidence: The claim is directly stated in the text with a specific frequency value.

claim: There was no significant deviation from Hardy-Weinberg equilibrium for the Sl or McC genotypes among controls.
source: There was no significant deviation from Hardy-Weinberg equilibrium for the Sl or McC genotypes among controls (Supplementary file 1C).
evidence: The claim is supported by reference to Supplementary file 1C containing statistical analysis.

claim: The Sl2/Sl2 genotype was associated with an adjusted Odds Ratio for severe malaria of 0.78 (95% CI 0.64–0.95; p=0.011) in the recessive form.
source: A significant protective association was observed for Sl2 in the recessive form (adjusted Odds Ratio (aOR) 0.78; 95% CI 0.64–0.95; p=0.011)
evidence: The claim is supported by statistical analysis results presented in the text.

claim: The Sl2/Sl2 genotype was associated with protection against cerebral malaria (aOR 0.67; 0.52–0.87; p=0.006).
source: A significant protective association was observed for Sl2 in the recessive form (adjusted Odds Ratio (aOR) 0.78; 95% CI 0.64–0.95; p=0.011), which was most marked for cerebral malaria (aOR 0.67; 0.52–0.87; p=0.006) (Figure 4 and Table 1).
evidence: The claim is supported by statistical analysis results presented in the text and shown in Figure 4 and Table 1.

claim: The Sl2/Sl2 genotype was associated with significant protection against death from severe malaria (aOR 0.50; 0.30–0.80; p=0.002).
source: The Sl2/Sl2 genotype was also associated with significant protection against death from severe malaria (aOR 0.50; 0.30–0.80; p=0.002)
evidence: The claim is supported by statistical analysis results presented in the text.

claim: The Sl2/Sl2 genotype was associated with protection against death among children admitted with cerebral malaria (aOR 0.44; 0.23–0.78; p=0.007).
source: The Sl2/Sl2 genotype was also associated with significant protection against death from severe malaria (aOR 0.50; 0.30–0.80; p=0.002), and death among children admitted with a specific diagnosis of cerebral malaria in the full adjusted analysis (aOR 0.44; 0.23–0.78; p=0.007) (Figure 4 and Table 1).
evidence: The claim is supported by statistical analysis results presented in the text and shown in Figure 4 and Table 1.

claim: There was a significant interaction between Sl2 and α+thalassaemia genotype, such that the protective associations of Sl2 were only seen in individuals of normal α-globin genotype.
source: Unexpectedly, we observed a significant interaction between Sl2 and α+thalassaemia genotype, such that the protective associations of Sl2 were only seen in individuals of normal α-globin genotype (Figure 5).
evidence: The claim is supported by statistical analysis results and shown in Figure 5.

claim: There was no evidence for an association between Sl2 and P. falciparum parasite density.
source: We found no evidence for an association between Sl2 and any other clinical form of severe malaria (Table 1), or with P. falciparum parasite density (Figure 6).
evidence: The claim is supported by reference to Figure 6 showing parasite density data.

claim: The McCb allele was associated with increased risk of cerebral malaria (aOR 1.19; 1.10–1.38; p=0.025) in the additive model.
source: Similar associations were seen in the full adjusted analysis, although this only reached statistical significance for cerebral malaria (aOR 1.19; 1.10–1.38; p=0.025 (additive model), Figure 4 and Table 1).
evidence: The claim is supported by statistical analysis results presented in the text and shown in Figure 4 and Table 1.

claim: There was no association between McCb and P. falciparum parasite density.
source: We found no association between McCb and any other clinical form of severe malaria (Table 1 and Supplementary file 1D) or with P. falciparum parasite density (Figure 6).
evidence: The claim is supported by reference to Figure 6 showing parasite density data.

claim: Sl and McC are 33 bp apart and are in linkage disequilibrium.
source: Sl and McC are 33 bp apart and are in linkage disequilibrium, with only three of four possible haplotypes observed in our data.
evidence: The claim is supported by data analysis results presented in the text.

claim: Only three of four possible haplotypes were observed in the Kenyan data.
source: Sl and McC are 33 bp apart and are in linkage disequilibrium, with only three of four possible haplotypes observed in our data.
evidence: The claim is supported by data analysis results presented in the text.

claim: The Sl2/McCa haplotype showed an additive protective association with severe malaria (aOR = 0.85; 0.75–0.96; p=0.007).
source: These analyses suggest an additive protective association with the Sl2/McCa haplotype (aOR = 0.85; 0.75–0.96; p=0.007)
evidence: The claim is supported by haplotype analysis results presented in the text.

claim: The Sl2 allele was associated with a >50% reduction in the incidence of uncomplicated malaria in the additive model.
source: After adjusting for variables known to influence malaria susceptibility, the Sl2 allele was associated with a >50% reduction in the incidence of uncomplicated malaria (additive model) (Table 2
evidence: The claim is supported by statistical analysis results presented in Table 2.

claim: A significant interaction was seen between Sl2 and α+thalassaemia in the longitudinal cohort study, such that the protective association of Sl2 was only demonstrated in children of normal α-globin genotype.
source: Once again, a significant interaction was seen with α+thalassaemia, such that the protective association of Sl2 was only demonstrated in children of normal α-globin genotype (Table 3).
evidence: The claim is supported by statistical analysis results presented in Table 3.

claim: There was no significant association between the McCb allele and uncomplicated malaria.
source: We found no significant association between the McCb allele and uncomplicated malaria (Table 2).
evidence: The claim is supported by reference to Table 2 showing statistical analysis results.

claim: McCb was associated with borderline significant protection against several common infectious diseases including LRTIs, URTIs and gastroenteritis.
source: McCb was associated with borderline significant protection against several common infectious diseases including LRTIs, URTIs and gastroenteritis (Table 2).
evidence: The claim is supported by statistical analysis results presented in Table 2.

claim: Sl2 was associated with a borderline reduced incidence of gastroenteritis.
source: Sl2 was associated with a borderline reduced incidence of gastroenteritis (Table 2).
evidence: The claim is supported by statistical analysis results presented in Table 2.

claim: The association of McCb with gastroenteritis was predominantly seen in children of normal α-globin genotype.
source: The association of McCb with gastroenteritis was predominantly seen in children of normal α-globin genotype, echoing the interaction seen with Sl2 and malaria.
evidence: The claim is supported by statistical analysis results presented in the text.

claim: The Sl2/Sl2 genotype was associated with protection against cerebral malaria in Mali (aOR 0.35, 95% CI 0.12–0.89, p=0.024).
source: Analysis of this small case-control study suggested a protective association between the Sl2/Sl2 genotype and cerebral malaria (aOR 0.35, 95% CI 0.12–0.89, p=0.024)
evidence: The claim is supported by statistical analysis results from the Malian case-control study.

claim: The Sl2/Sl2-McCa/McCa genotype combination was associated with protection against cerebral malaria in Mali (aOR 0.14, 95% CI 0.02–0.84, p=0.031).
source: the Sl2/Sl2-McCa/McCa genotype combination was associated with protection against cerebral malaria (aOR 0.14, 95% CI 0.02–0.84, p=0.031, Appendix 1).
evidence: The claim is supported by statistical analysis results presented in Appendix 1.

claim: The median rosette frequency was significantly lower in P. falciparum isolates from malaria patients with one or more Sl2 alleles than in isolates from Sl1/Sl1 donors.
source: The median rosette frequency (percentage of iRBC that form rosettes) was significantly lower in P. falciparum isolates from malaria patients with one or more Sl2 alleles than in isolates from Sl1/Sl1 donors (Figure 7)
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 7.

claim: McC genotype had no significant associations with P. falciparum rosette frequency.
source: whereas McC genotype had no significant associations with P. falciparum rosette frequency (Figure 7).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 7.

claim: The protective association between Sl2 and cerebral malaria was first reported in a small case-control study from western Kenya.
source: The protective association between Sl2 and cerebral malaria was first reported in a small case-control study from western Kenya (Thathy et al., 2005)
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Thathy et al., 2005.

claim: This study is the first adequately powered independent sample set that replicates the protective association between Sl2 and cerebral malaria.
source: Hence, our study is the first adequately powered independent sample set that replicates the protective association between Sl2 and cerebral malaria.
evidence: The claim is based on the authors' interpretation of their study results in the context of previous literature.

claim: Other studies found no consistent significant associations between Sl genotypes and severe malaria.
source: Other studies found no consistent significant associations between Sl genotypes and severe malaria (Zimmerman et al., 2003; Hansson et al., 2013; Jallow et al., 2009; Manjurano et al., 2012; Toure et al., 2012; Rockett et al., 2014)
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to multiple studies.

claim: A weak association between McCb and an increased odds ratio for cerebral malaria was shown in a multi-centre study.
source: A weak association between McCb and an increased odds ratio for cerebral malaria was shown in the multi-centre study (Rockett et al., 2014).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Rockett et al., 2014.

claim: The protective association of Sl2 was observed most clearly when both McCb and α+thalassaemia genotypes were included in the statistical model.
source: The protective association of Sl2 was observed most clearly when both McCb and α+thalassaemia genotypes were included in the statistical model, something that has not been considered in previous studies.
evidence: The claim is based on the authors' analysis and comparison with previous studies.

claim: The interaction between Sl2 and α+thalassaemia is reminiscent of the epistatic interactions that have been observed between α+thalassaemia and other malaria-protective polymorphisms including sickle cell trait (HbAS) and haptoglobin.
source: The interaction we describe here between Sl2 and α+thalassaemia is reminiscent of the epistatic interactions that have been observed between α+thalassaemia and other malaria-protective polymorphisms including sickle cell trait (HbAS) (Williams et al., 2005a) and haptoglobin (Atkinson et al., 2014).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Williams et al., 2005a and Atkinson et al., 2014.

claim: α+thalassaemia may have a broad effect on multiple malaria-protective polymorphisms, influencing their restricted global frequencies.
source: It is possible, therefore, that α+thalassaemia has a broad effect on multiple malaria-protective polymorphisms, influencing their restricted global frequencies (Penman et al., 2009)
evidence: The claim is speculative and supported by a citation to Penman et al., 2009.

claim: Recent large genetic association studies on malaria do not include data on α+thalassaemia, because the causal deletions are not typed on automated platforms.
source: Recent large genetic association studies on malaria do not include data on α+thalassaemia, because the causal deletions are not typed on automated platforms (Rockett et al., 2014), instead requiring manual genotyping using labour-intensive PCR-based methods (Chong et al., 2000).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Rockett et al., 2014 and Chong et al., 2000.

claim: Previous in vitro experiments showed that CR1 is a receptor for P. falciparum rosetting on uninfected RBCs.
source: Previous in vitro experiments showed that CR1 is a receptor for P. falciparum rosetting on uninfected RBCs, and that RBCs serologically typed as negative for the Sl1 antigen (likely to be from donors with Sl1/Sl2 or Sl2/Sl2 genotypes) (Moulds et al., 2001) show reduced binding to the parasite rosetting ligand PfEMP1 (Rowe et al., 1997) .
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Moulds et al., 2001 and Rowe et al., 1997.

claim: RBCs serologically typed as negative for the Sl1 antigen show reduced binding to the parasite rosetting ligand PfEMP1.
source: Previous in vitro experiments showed that CR1 is a receptor for P. falciparum rosetting on uninfected RBCs, and that RBCs serologically typed as negative for the Sl1 antigen (likely to be from donors with Sl1/Sl2 or Sl2/Sl2 genotypes) (Moulds et al., 2001) show reduced binding to the parasite rosetting ligand PfEMP1 (Rowe et al., 1997) .
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Moulds et al., 2001 and Rowe et al., 1997.

claim: Reduced rosetting and subsequent reduced microvascular obstruction may in part explain the protective association of Sl2 against cerebral malaria.
source: Therefore, similar to HbC (Fairhurst et al., 2005), blood group O (Rowe et al., 2007) and RBC CR1 deficiency (Cockburn et al., 2004), it is possible that reduced rosetting and subsequent reduced microvascular obstruction (Kaul et al., 1991) may in part explain the protective association of Sl2 against cerebral malaria.
evidence: The claim is speculative and supported by citations to multiple studies.

claim: The Knops polymorphisms may be associated with broader effects on the complement regulatory functions of CR1.
source: However, given the protective association of Sl2 with uncomplicated malaria, and the possible associations of Sl2 and McCb with other common childhood infections, it seems likely that the Knops polymorphisms may be associated with broader effects, for example on the complement regulatory functions of CR1.
evidence: The claim is speculative based on the study findings.

claim: Neither cofactor activity for the breakdown of C3b and C4b nor binding to C1q are influenced by the Sl2 and McCb mutations.
source: Previously, we have shown that neither cofactor activity for the breakdown of C3b and C4b nor binding to C1q are influenced by the Sl2 and McCb mutations (Tetteh-Quarcoo et al., 2012).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Tetteh-Quarcoo et al., 2012.

claim: There is no association between Knops genotype and CR1 clustering on erythrocytes.
source: In addition, we can find no association between Knops genotype and CR1 clustering on erythrocytes (Paccaud et al., 1988; Swann et al., 2017).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Paccaud et al., 1988 and Swann et al., 2017.

claim: Two high frequency CR1 polymorphisms have opposing associations with cerebral malaria and death in Kenyan children.
source: In conclusion, we show that two high frequency CR1 polymorphisms have opposing associations with cerebral malaria and death in Kenyan children.
evidence: The claim summarizes the main findings of the study.

claim: The Sl2 allele may have reached high frequency in African populations by conferring a protective advantage against cerebral malaria.
source: While the Sl2 allele may have reached high frequency in African populations by conferring a protective advantage against cerebral malaria, our data suggest that McCb arose due to a survival advantage afforded against other non-malarial infections (Noumsi et al., 2011; Fitness et al., 2004).
evidence: The claim is speculative and supported by citations to Noumsi et al., 2011 and Fitness et al., 2004.

claim: McCb arose due to a survival advantage afforded against other non-malarial infections.
source: While the Sl2 allele may have reached high frequency in African populations by conferring a protective advantage against cerebral malaria, our data suggest that McCb arose due to a survival advantage afforded against other non-malarial infections (Noumsi et al., 2011; Fitness et al., 2004).
evidence: The claim is speculative and supported by citations to Noumsi et al., 2011 and Fitness et al., 2004.

claim: Sl2 may in part protect against cerebral malaria by reducing rosetting, but additional effects seem likely.
source: Sl2 may in part protect against cerebral malaria by reducing rosetting, but additional effects seem likely.
evidence: The claim is speculative based on the study findings.

claim: Future epidemiological studies should account for the effect of α+thalassaemia on the associations between Sl2 and McCb on malaria and other infectious diseases.
source: Future epidemiological studies should account for the effect of α+thalassaemia on the associations between Sl2 and McCb on malaria and other infectious diseases.
evidence: The claim is a recommendation based on the study findings.

claim: Malaria transmission is seasonal in the Kilifi region following the long and short rains.
source: Malaria transmission is seasonal in this region following the long and short rains.
evidence: The claim is based on established knowledge about the study area.

claim: An Entomological Inoculation Rate (EIR) of up to 50 infective bites per person per year was measured in the late 1990s in Kilifi.
source: An Entomological Inoculation Rate (EIR) of up to 50 infective bites per person per year was measured in the late 1990s (Mbogo et al., 2003)
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Mbogo et al., 2003.

claim: Malaria transmission has declined in Kilifi since the late 1990s.
source: An Entomological Inoculation Rate (EIR) of up to 50 infective bites per person per year was measured in the late 1990s (Mbogo et al., 2003), but transmission has since declined (O'Meara et al., 2008).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to O'Meara et al., 2008.

claim: Between January 2001 and January 2008, children aged <14 years who were admitted to KCH with severe malaria were recruited as cases.
source: Between January 2001 and January 2008, children aged <14 years who were admitted to KCH with severe malaria were recruited as cases, as described previously (Rockett et al., 2014)
evidence: The claim describes the study design and is supported by a citation to Rockett et al., 2014.

claim: Controls consisted of children 3–12 months of age who were born consecutively within the KHDSS study area between August 2006 and September 2010.
source: Controls (n = 3829) consisted of children 3–12 months of age who were born consecutively within the KHDSS study area between August 2006 and September 2010 and were recruited to an ongoing genetic cohort study (Williams et al., 2009).
evidence: The claim describes the study design and is supported by a citation to Williams et al., 2009.

claim: The use of controls who are considerably younger than cases has been widely used in African genetic association studies.
source: However, this method (using cord blood or infant samples as controls) has been widely used in African genetic association studies (e.g. [Band et al., 2013; Busby et al., 2016; Clarke et al., 2017])
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to multiple studies.

claim: The ectodomain of CR1 is composed of 30 Complement Control Protein (CCP) domains which are organized into four 'Long Homologous Repeats' (LHR).
source: The ectodomain of CR1 is composed of 30 Complement Control Protein (CCP) domains which are organized into four 'Long Homologous Repeats' (LHR).
evidence: The claim is shown in Figure 1 and adapted from Schmidt et al. (2015) and Krych-Goldberg et al. (2002).

claim: The single-nucleotide polymorphisms determining the Sl and McC antigens of the Knops blood group system are found in CCP 25 in LHR-D.
source: The single-nucleotide polymorphisms determining the Sl and McC antigens of the Knops blood group system are found in CCP 25 in LHR-D (red).
evidence: The claim is shown in Figure 1.

claim: Site 1 of CR1 has decay accelerating activity for C3 convertases and binds the complement component C4b and the P. falciparum invasion ligand PfRH4.
source: Various functions have been mapped to different regions of CR1, including Site 1 (decay accelerating activity for C3 convertases; binding of the complement component C4b and the P. falciparum invasion ligand PfRH4)
evidence: The claim is shown in Figure 1 and adapted from Schmidt et al. (2015) and Krych-Goldberg et al. (2002).

claim: Site 2 of CR1 has cofactor activity for Factor I and binds C3b, C4b and P. falciparum rosetting.
source: and Site 2 (cofactor activity for Factor I; binding of C3b and C4b and P. falciparum rosetting).

claim: LHR-D is thought to bind C1q and Mannose Binding lectin (MBL), but the specific binding sites have not been mapped.
source: LHR-D is thought to bind C1q and Mannose Binding lectin (MBL), but the specific binding sites have not been mapped.
